conceptTag: Charm pricing and the left-digit effect
readerTitle: $9.99 vs $10.00. One cent. Why does the gap feel bigger?
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Anderson & Simester 2003, Lacetera et al. 2012, Wadhwa & Zhang 2015) + 실제 기업 (JCPenney 2012) + 가상 사례 (웨딩 촬영, 충전기)
insight: 가격 끝자리는 "싸다" 또는 "믿을 만하다"는 메시지를 보낸다.
misconception: $9.99가 싸 보이는 건 앵커링 때문이다. 언제나 .99로 끝나는 가격이 낫다.

sources.text: Anderson & Simester (2003). Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales. Quantitative Marketing and Economics.
Thomas & Morwitz (2005). Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition. J. of Consumer Research.
Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor (2012). Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market. American Economic Review.
Wadhwa & Zhang (2015). This Number Just Feels Right. J. of Consumer Research.

factChecks.note: 처음 받은 목업의 퀴즈("$9.99가 싸게 느껴지는 건 가격 앵커링 때문")는 개념이 틀렸습니다. 이 레슨의 9번 카드에서 그 혼동 자체를 문제로 만들었습니다.
JCPenney 매출 감소(약 25%)는 FY2011 $17.26B → FY2012 $12.98B 기준입니다. 원인은 단수가격 폐지 하나가 아니라 세일·쿠폰 폐지와 함께 일어났다는 점을 카드에 명시했습니다.
JCPenney 로고와 매장 사진은 상표 사용 여부를 검토해야 합니다. 일러스트로 대체하는 것을 권장합니다.

cards.title: $9.99 vs $10.00. One cent. Why does the gap feel bigger?
body: Retailers have used prices ending in 9 for over a century. Is it a real effect, or a habit nobody questions?
Let's test your instinct against real data.

image.label: Sneaker with $9.99 and $10.00 tags
image.brief: 목업 3번 화면처럼 흰 스니커즈 위에 빨간 "$9.99" 태그, 옆에 회색 "$10.00" 태그. 두 태그의 크기는 같게.

cards.title: Three catalogs, three prices.
body: A US clothing retailer mailed different versions of its catalog to different customers. The same women's dress was listed at **$34**, **$39**, or **$44**.
Which price sold the most dresses?

options.feedback: Reasonable guess, but no. The $34 version sold fewer dresses than the $39 one, even though it was $5 cheaper.
Correct. In Anderson and Simester's 2003 field experiment, the $39 dress outsold both $34 and $44. The higher price sold more units than the lower one.

options.text: $44, because a higher price signals quality
options.feedback: It sold the fewest. Quality signals matter, but here the price ending in 9 won.

cards.title: The left-digit effect
body: We read prices left to right and give the first digit the most weight. $2.99 gets filed as "two-something" before we finish reading it.
So $2.99 vs $3.00 can feel like a one-dollar gap, not a one-cent gap. Researchers call this the **left-digit effect**. Prices ending in .99 or .95 are called **charm prices**.

image.label: Big "2" and small ".99"
image.brief: 타이포그래피 비주얼. 아주 큰 "2"와 작은 ".99". 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 시선이 흐르며 점점 흐려지는 그라데이션.

cards.title: A 9 also says "deal".
body: In the same research, Anderson and Simester found that prices ending in 9 also work as a **signal**. Shoppers have learned that 9-endings often show up on sale items.
That's useful for a discount store. It's a problem when you want to look premium. We'll come back to that in two cards.

cards.title: It even moves used-car prices.
body: Economists Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor studied more than 22 million used-car auction sales. A car with 79,900 miles and one with 80,100 miles are practically the same car.
Prices didn't fall smoothly with mileage. They dropped in sudden steps at every 10,000-mile mark. Buyers read odometers the way shoppers read price tags: left digit first.

image.label: Odometers: 79,900 vs 80,100
image.brief: 자동차 주행거리계 두 개를 나란히. "79,900"과 "80,100". 두 번째 계기판 아래에 작은 가격 하락 화살표.

cards.title: JCPenney dropped the .99s. Then the shoppers left.
body: In 2012, new CEO Ron Johnson replaced constant sales and coupons with "Fair and Square" everyday pricing, using whole-dollar prices like $10 instead of $9.99.
Revenue fell about 25% that year. Johnson was out by April 2013.
Dropping .99 wasn't the only cause. Removing sales also removed the "was" prices that anchored every deal (Lesson 1). Shoppers lost both signals at once.

image.label: Department store price tags: $9.99 → $10
image.brief: 백화점 가격표가 "$9.99"에서 "$10"으로 바뀌는 비포/애프터 일러스트. 실제 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Round prices win when the purchase is emotional.
body: A 2015 study by Monica Wadhwa and Kuangjie Zhang found that round prices like $100 feel "right" for purchases driven by feelings, while precise prices like $98.76 fit purchases driven by calculation.
That's why luxury watches, wedding packages and tasting menus rarely end in .99. A 9 says "bargain", which is the wrong message for them.

cards.title: Two products, two price endings.
body: You're pricing a **premium wedding photography package** at around $3,000 and a **phone charger** sold on Amazon at around $20.
Which combination fits best?

options.feedback: The charger is right. But $2,999 tells a couple they're getting a deal on their wedding photos, which is the wrong message for a premium service.
Yes. A round price for the emotional, high-trust purchase. A charm price for the product people compare on a search results page.
The wedding price is right. The charger sits next to dozens of near-identical listings, where $19.99 reads as noticeably cheaper than $20.

cards.title: Is $9.99 vs $10 an example of price anchoring?
body: These two ideas get mixed up a lot, even in professional marketing content.

options.feedback: Not quite. Anchoring needs a reference number that a price is compared to, like the $429 bread maker. $9.99 works on its own because of how we read digits. That's the left-digit effect.
Right. Anchoring is comparison with a reference number. The left-digit effect is about how we read the number itself.

cards.title: Match the price ending to the message.
body: **.99** says value and deal. Use it where customers compare prices side by side.
**Round numbers** say quality and confidence. Use them where the purchase is emotional or premium.
**Try it today:** list your top 3 products. Does each price ending send the message you want?
